**(C)** \(E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}Kr}\)

Consider an infinitely long charged cylinder carrying a charge \(\lambda\) per unit length, placed in a medium of dielectric constant \(K\). Take as the Gaussian surface a coaxial cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(l\), with \(r\) greater than the radius of the charged cylinder.

By symmetry the field is radial and has the same magnitude at every point of the curved surface, while it is parallel to the two flat end faces, so those contribute no flux.

Flux through the curved surface \(= E \times 2\pi rl\)

Charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface \(= \lambda l\)

By Gauss' law applied in the medium,

\(E \times 2\pi rl = \dfrac{\lambda l}{K\epsilon_{0}}\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}Kr}\)

The field of a line charge therefore falls off as \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), not as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\). The three rejected expressions all vary as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\) and place \(\epsilon_{0}\) in the numerator instead of the denominator, so none of them reduces to \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}r}\) in free space, where \(K = 1\).

**(A)** \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\left(\dfrac{R}{r}\right)^{2}\)

For a charged conducting sphere the whole charge resides on its outer surface, so with surface charge density \(\sigma\) the total charge on a sphere of radius \(R\) is

\(q = \sigma \times 4\pi R^{2}\)

Apply Gauss' law to a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius \(r\) drawn outside the sphere, in a medium of permittivity \(\epsilon\). By symmetry the field is radial and uniform over this surface, so

\(E \times 4\pi r^{2} = \dfrac{q}{\epsilon}\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon r^{2}} = \dfrac{\sigma \times 4\pi R^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon r^{2}}\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\left(\dfrac{R}{r}\right)^{2}\)

Check at the surface: putting \(r = R\) gives \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\), which is the field just outside a charged conductor, as it must be. The expression with the ratio inverted would grow with distance instead of falling; the one whose bracket is \(\dfrac{R}{r^{2}}\) is not dimensionless, so it cannot multiply \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\) to give a field; and the one with \(\sigma\) and \(\epsilon\) interchanged does not even have the dimensions of an electric field.
twin: A sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of \( 1\,\mu\text{C} \). Calculate the electric field (i) at a distance of 30 cm from the center of the sphere (ii) at the surface of the sphere and (iii) at a distance of 5 cm from the center of the sphere.

**(B)** increase in dielectric constant.

For a point outside a charged sphere carrying a charge \(q\), placed in a medium of dielectric constant \(K\), the electric intensity at a distance \(r\) from the centre is

\(E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}Kr^{2}}\)

Reading the dependence on each quantity in turn:

\(E \propto q\), so increasing the charge on the sphere INCREASES \(E\);

\(E \propto \dfrac{1}{K}\), so increasing the dielectric constant of the surrounding medium DECREASES \(E\);

\(E \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\), so decreasing the distance from the centre, or decreasing the square of that distance, INCREASES \(E\).

\(\therefore\) of the four changes listed, the only one that makes \(E\) smaller is an increase in the dielectric constant of the medium.

Given: area \(A = 40\text{ cm}^{2} = 40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^{2} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^{2}\), charge \(q = 0.2\,\mu\text{C} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ C}\), \(\epsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\) S.I. units.

**Surface charge density.**

\(\sigma = \dfrac{q}{A} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = 5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ C/m}^{2}\)

**Electric intensity just outside the surface.** For a charged conductor of any shape the field just outside the surface is normal to it. Applying Gauss' law to a small pill-box straddling the surface, the flat face lying inside the conductor contributes nothing because the field inside a conductor is zero, so the whole flux \(E\,\mathrm{d}A\) leaves through the outer face and

\(E\,\mathrm{d}A = \dfrac{\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A}{\epsilon_{0}}\)

\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-5}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}}\)

\(\therefore E = 5.65 \times 10^{6}\text{ N/C}\)

**Mechanical force per unit area.** Each element of the charged surface is pushed outward by the field of the rest of the conductor. The field acting on the surface charge itself is the mean of the field just inside, which is zero, and the field just outside, which is \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0}}\), that is \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_{0}}\). Hence the outward force per unit area is

\(f = \sigma \times \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2\epsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{\left(5 \times 10^{-5}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-9}}{1.77 \times 10^{-11}}\)

\(\therefore f = 141.2\text{ N/m}^{2}\)

Check: the same quantity can be written as \(f = \dfrac{1}{2}\sigma E = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-5} \times 5.65 \times 10^{6} = 141.2\text{ N/m}^{2}\), the same value by an independent route.

Given: surface charge density \(\sigma = 8.85\,\mu\text{C/m}^{2} = 8.85 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C/m}^{2}\), \(\epsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^{2}/\text{Nm}^{2}\).

A large charged plane sheet produces a field on both sides of itself. Take as the Gaussian surface a cylindrical pill-box of cross-sectional area \(A\) piercing the sheet, with its two flat faces parallel to the sheet and equidistant from it. The field is normal to the sheet, so the curved surface contributes no flux and the flux leaves through both flat faces:

\(E \times 2A = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_{0}}\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_{0}}\)

Substituting the given values,

\(E = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}\)

\(\therefore E = 5 \times 10^{5}\text{ N/C}\)

The field is directed normally away from the sheet, and being independent of the distance from it, it has this same value at every point near the middle of the sheet.

Check: working backwards, \(\sigma = 2\epsilon_{0}E = 2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 10^{5} = 8.85 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C/m}^{2}\), the charge density given.

**Energy stored in a charged capacitor.**

Let a capacitor of capacitance \(C\) be charged by transferring charge from one plate to the other. Suppose that at some stage of the charging the capacitor carries a charge \(q\), so that the potential difference across it at that instant is

\(v = \dfrac{q}{C}\)

To transfer a further small charge \(\mathrm{d}q\) against this potential difference, the work that must be done is

\(\mathrm{d}W = v\,\mathrm{d}q = \dfrac{q}{C}\,\mathrm{d}q\)

The total work done in charging the capacitor from zero charge up to a final charge \(Q\) is therefore

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q}\dfrac{q}{C}\,\mathrm{d}q = \dfrac{1}{C}\left[\dfrac{q^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{Q} = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}\)

This work is stored in the capacitor as electrostatic potential energy \(U\):

\(\therefore U = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}QV\)

the three forms following from one another through \(Q = CV\).

**Numerical.** Given: radius of the ball \(R = 15\text{ cm} = 0.15\text{ m}\), charge \(q = 2\,\mu\text{C} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}\), distance of the point from the centre \(r = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\).

Since \(r > R\), the point lies outside the ball, and the entire charge of a spherical conductor acts as though it were concentrated at its centre. Hence

\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.20)^{2}} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{4}}{0.04}\)

\(\therefore E = 4.5 \times 10^{5}\text{ N/C}\)

Check: the field at the surface of the same ball would be \(\dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^{2}} = 8 \times 10^{5}\text{ N/C}\), and the ratio \(\dfrac{8 \times 10^{5}}{4.5 \times 10^{5}} = 1.78\), which equals \(\left(\dfrac{0.20}{0.15}\right)^{2}\) as the inverse-square law requires.

**(D)** \(\dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\)

Potential gradient is the rate of change of electric potential with distance,

\(\text{potential gradient} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}\)

so its unit is the unit of potential divided by the unit of distance. In S.I. the unit of potential is the volt and the unit of distance is the metre, giving \(\text{V m}^{-1}\), that is \(\dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\).

This is also the S.I. unit of electric field intensity, as it must be, since \(E = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}\). Among the units rejected, two are products of potential and length rather than ratios, and so are units of a quantity of an altogether different kind; the remaining ratio is built on the centimetre, which is a C.G.S. unit and not the S.I. unit of length.

The magnitude of the electric field intensity at a point is equal to the potential gradient at that point, and the field is directed opposite to the gradient:

\(E = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}\)

Here \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}\) is the potential gradient, that is the rate of change of electric potential \(V\) with distance \(r\) measured along the direction of the field, and \(E\) is the electric field intensity at that point.

In three dimensions the same relation is written

\(\vec{E} = -\left(\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)\)

The negative sign shows that the electric field is directed from a region of higher potential towards a region of lower potential, that is, along the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly. Both sides of the relation have the S.I. unit \(\text{V m}^{-1}\), which is the same as \(\text{N C}^{-1}\).

**(C)** electric potential

The electric potential at a point in an electric field is defined as the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, without acceleration, against the electric field:

\(V = \dfrac{W}{q_{0}}\)

where \(W\) is the work done in bringing a small positive test charge \(q_{0}\) from infinity up to the point. Infinity is taken as the position of zero potential, and the S.I. unit of potential is the volt, \(1\text{ V} = 1\text{ J C}^{-1}\).

Of the other quantities named, electric flux is the measure of the number of lines of force crossing a given area, \(\Phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}\); gravitational potential is the work done in bringing unit MASS from infinity to a point in a gravitational field; and magnetic potential belongs to a magnetic field, not to the electric field described in the question.

**(C)** \(\dfrac{1}{r}\)

The electric potential at a distance \(r\) from a point charge \(q\) placed in free space is

\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q}{r}\)

For a given charge the factor \(\dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\) is a constant, so

\(\therefore V \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\)

The potential thus falls to half its value when the distance from the charge is doubled, and tends to zero as \(r\) tends to infinity, which is the zero level chosen for potential. It is the electric FIELD of a point charge, \(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}}\), that varies as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\); and a potential proportional to \(r\) or to \(r^{2}\) would grow without limit far from the charge instead of vanishing there.

Given: capacity of the parallel plate air condenser \(C = 20\,\mu\text{F}\).

For a parallel plate condenser with air between the plates,

\(C = \dfrac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}\)

Each of the two changes below is made to this original condenser.

**i. The distance between the plates is doubled.** The area of the plates and the medium are unchanged, so \(C \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\). Putting \(d' = 2d\),

\(\dfrac{C'}{C} = \dfrac{d}{d'} = \dfrac{d}{2d} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore C' = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\,\mu\text{F}\)

**ii. A marble slab of dielectric constant 8 is introduced between the plates.** The slab fills the space between the plates, so \(A\) and \(d\) are unchanged while the medium changes from air to marble, and

\(C'' = \dfrac{k\epsilon_{0}A}{d} = kC\)

\(\therefore C'' = 8 \times 20 = 160\,\mu\text{F}\)

Check: the two changes act on the capacity in opposite senses and in the expected ratios, \(\dfrac{C'}{C} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{C''}{C} = 8\); had both changes been made together the capacity would have been \(\dfrac{8 \times 20}{2} = 80\,\mu\text{F}\).

**Capacitance of a capacitor.** When one conductor of a capacitor is given a charge \(+Q\) and the other an equal and opposite charge \(-Q\), the potential difference \(V\) set up between the two conductors is found to be directly proportional to that charge:

\(Q \propto V\), so \(Q = CV\)

The constant of proportionality \(C\) is called the capacitance of the capacitor.

\(\therefore C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\)

The capacitance of a capacitor is therefore defined as the ratio of the magnitude of the charge on either of its conductors to the magnitude of the potential difference between the two conductors. Equivalently, it is the charge required to raise the potential difference between the conductors by unity. It depends only on the size and shape of the conductors, on their separation and on the medium between them, and not on the charge given to them.

**S.I. unit.** The S.I. unit of capacitance is the farad, symbol F.

\(1\text{ farad} = \dfrac{1\text{ coulomb}}{1\text{ volt}}\)

A capacitor has a capacitance of one farad if a charge of one coulomb given to it raises the potential difference across it by one volt. The farad is inconveniently large for practical work, so the submultiples microfarad, \(1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), and picofarad, \(1\text{ pF} = 10^{-12}\text{ F}\), are the units in common use.

Given: capacity of the capacitor with the dielectric \(C_{m} = 40\,\mu\text{F}\), dielectric constant \(k = 5\).

For a parallel plate capacitor, filling the space between the plates completely with a dielectric of constant \(k\) multiplies the capacitance by \(k\), because the medium enters the expression for the capacitance and nothing else changes:

\(C_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}\) and \(C_{m} = \dfrac{k\epsilon_{0}A}{d} = kC_{\text{air}}\)

Removing the dielectric therefore divides the capacity by \(k\):

\(\therefore C_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{C_{m}}{k} = \dfrac{40}{5}\)

\(\therefore C_{\text{air}} = 8\,\mu\text{F}\)

Check: putting the dielectric of constant 5 back gives \(5 \times 8 = 40\,\mu\text{F}\), the capacity stated in the question.

**Parallel plate capacitor.** A parallel plate capacitor consists of two plane conducting plates, each of area \(A\), held parallel to each other and separated by a small distance \(d\), the space between them being filled with air or with a dielectric.

One plate is given a charge \(+Q\) and the other an equal and opposite charge \(-Q\). If the separation is small compared with the size of the plates, the charge spreads uniformly over the facing surfaces with surface density

\(\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{A}\)

and the field between the plates is uniform and directed from the positive plate to the negative plate:

\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{Q}{\epsilon_{0}A}\)

Outside the pair of plates the fields due to the two plates are equal and opposite, so the field there is zero. Since the field between the plates is uniform, the potential difference between them is

\(V = Ed = \dfrac{Qd}{\epsilon_{0}A}\)

\(\therefore C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}\)

and when a dielectric of constant \(k\) fills the space between the plates, \(C = \dfrac{k\epsilon_{0}A}{d}\). The capacitance thus depends only on the area of the plates, their separation and the medium between them, and not on the charge given to them.

**Two applications.**

1. It stores electric charge and electrostatic energy, as in the capacitor that stores the energy afterwards discharged through the flash lamp of a camera.
2. A parallel plate capacitor of variable capacitance, obtained by changing the effective overlap of the plates, is used to tune a radio receiver to the frequency of a chosen station.

A dielectric is an insulator that can be polarised by an external electric field. Dielectrics are of two kinds, according to the nature of their molecules.

**Non-polar dielectrics.** In a non-polar dielectric the centre of the positive charge of each molecule coincides with the centre of its negative charge, so the molecule has NO permanent electric dipole moment. When such a dielectric is placed in an external electric field the two centres are pulled apart slightly in opposite directions, and each molecule acquires an INDUCED dipole moment directed along the field. The induced moment disappears as soon as the field is removed. Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane and benzene are non-polar.

**Polar dielectrics.** In a polar dielectric the centre of the positive charge of a molecule does not coincide with the centre of its negative charge, so every molecule possesses a PERMANENT electric dipole moment even when no external field is applied. In the absence of a field these molecular dipoles point in random directions on account of thermal agitation, so the dielectric as a whole shows no net dipole moment. In an external field they tend to turn into alignment with the field and the dielectric becomes polarised, the alignment being more complete the stronger the field and the lower the temperature. Water, hydrogen chloride, ammonia and alcohol are polar.

In both kinds the polarisation sets up within the material a field opposing the applied field, which is why the net field inside a dielectric is smaller than the applied field by the factor \(k\), the dielectric constant of the material.

Given: area of each plate \(A = 6\text{ cm}^{2} = 6 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^{2}\), plate separation \(d = 3\text{ mm} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\), air between the plates so that \(k = 1\), and \(\epsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^{2}/\text{Nm}^{2}\).

For a parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates,

\(C = \dfrac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d} = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 6 \times 10^{-4}}{3 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(= 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.2\)

\(\therefore C = 1.77 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F} = 1.77\text{ pF}\)

Check on the magnitude: the plates are small and their separation is comparatively large, so a capacitance of the order of a picofarad is to be expected. Enlarging the plates tenfold, or reducing the separation tenfold, would each raise the capacitance to \(1.77 \times 10^{-11}\text{ F}\), since \(C \propto A\) and \(C \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\).

**Two capacitors in series.** Let two capacitors of capacitances \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) be joined end to end and the combination connected across a source maintaining a potential difference \(V\).

Let a charge \(+Q\) be given to the outer plate of the first capacitor. It induces a charge \(-Q\) on the plate facing it. The middle section, formed by the second plate of the first capacitor and the first plate of the second capacitor joined by a conducting wire, is isolated and was uncharged to begin with, so its total charge must remain zero; hence a charge \(+Q\) appears on the first plate of the second capacitor, which in turn induces \(-Q\) on the plate facing it. Therefore in a series combination EVERY capacitor carries the same charge \(Q\).

The potential differences across the two capacitors are

\(V_{1} = \dfrac{Q}{C_{1}}\) and \(V_{2} = \dfrac{Q}{C_{2}}\)

The applied potential difference is shared between the two capacitors:

\(V = V_{1} + V_{2}\)

Let \(C_{s}\) be the capacitance of a single capacitor that would store the same charge \(Q\) at the same applied potential difference \(V\). Then \(V = \dfrac{Q}{C_{s}}\), and substituting the three potential differences,

\(\dfrac{Q}{C_{s}} = \dfrac{Q}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{Q}{C_{2}}\)

Dividing throughout by \(Q\),

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{C_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}}\)

\(\therefore C_{s} = \dfrac{C_{1}C_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}}\)

Since \(\dfrac{1}{C_{s}}\) is greater than either \(\dfrac{1}{C_{1}}\) or \(\dfrac{1}{C_{2}}\), the equivalent capacitance of a series combination is smaller than the smaller of the two capacitances.

**(D)** four times the initial energy

The energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance \(C\) carrying a charge \(Q\) is

\(U = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}\)

The capacitor here is the same one throughout, so \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F}\) is unchanged and

\(U \propto Q^{2}\)

Let the charge be doubled, so that \(Q_{2} = 2Q_{1}\). Then

\(\dfrac{U_{2}}{U_{1}} = \dfrac{Q_{2}^{2}}{Q_{1}^{2}} = \left(\dfrac{2Q_{1}}{Q_{1}}\right)^{2} = 4\)

\(\therefore U_{2} = 4U_{1}\)

Check with numbers: a charge \(Q_{1} = 10\,\mu\text{C}\) on \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F}\) stores \(U_{1} = \dfrac{\left(10 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}\), while \(Q_{2} = 20\,\mu\text{C}\) stores \(U_{2} = \dfrac{\left(20 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ J}\), which is four times \(U_{1}\). The energy cannot be zero, halved or merely doubled, because it depends on the SQUARE of the charge and not on its first power.

Given: side of the cube \(a = 1\text{ cm} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}\), electric field intensity \(E = 300\text{ V/m}\), dielectric constant of marble \(k = 8\), \(\epsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^{2}/\text{Nm}^{2}\). The field \(E\) is taken to be the field within the marble itself.

**Energy density.** The energy stored per unit volume of a medium of permittivity \(\epsilon = k\epsilon_{0}\) carrying an electric field \(E\) is

\(u = \dfrac{1}{2}\epsilon E^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}k\epsilon_{0}E^{2}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times (300)^{2}\)

\(= 3.54 \times 10^{-11} \times 9 \times 10^{4}\)

\(= 3.186 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J/m}^{3}\)

**Volume of the cube.**

\(V = a^{3} = \left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{3} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^{3}\)

**Energy contained in the cube.**

\(U = uV = 3.186 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}\)

\(\therefore U = 3.186 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J}\)

Check: with air in place of the marble the same cube in the same field would hold \(\dfrac{3.186 \times 10^{-12}}{8} = 3.98 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}\), so filling it with a dielectric of constant 8 raises the stored energy eightfold, exactly as \(u \propto k\) requires.

Given: \(C_{1} = 5\,\mu\text{F}\) and \(C_{2} = 10\,\mu\text{F}\), connected in series.

In a series combination each capacitor carries the same charge and the applied potential difference is shared between them, so the reciprocals of the capacitances add:

\(\dfrac{1}{C_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 + 1}{10} = \dfrac{3}{10}\)

\(\therefore C_{s} = \dfrac{10}{3}\)

\(\therefore C_{s} = 3.33\,\mu\text{F}\)

Check: the same value follows from \(C_{s} = \dfrac{C_{1}C_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}} = \dfrac{5 \times 10}{5 + 10} = \dfrac{50}{15} = 3.33\,\mu\text{F}\), and it is smaller than \(5\,\mu\text{F}\), as the resultant capacity of a series combination must be.

**Four uses of the Van de Graaff generator.**

1. It develops the very high potential difference, of the order of millions of volts, that is needed to accelerate charged particles such as protons, deuterons and heavy ions to high energies.
2. The high-energy particles so obtained are used to bombard nuclei, and hence to study nuclear reactions and artificial nuclear disintegration.
3. It serves as the pre-accelerator, or injector, that feeds particles into larger machines such as the linear accelerator.
4. The high potential difference it develops is applied to X-ray tubes to produce hard X-rays, which are used in radiotherapy and in the industrial radiography of castings and welds.

**Displacement current.** Given: rate of change of the electric field intensity \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = 2 \times 10^{11}\text{ V m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\), area of each plate \(A = 20\text{ cm}^{2} = 20 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^{2} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^{2}\), air between the plates, \(\epsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^{2}/\text{Nm}^{2}\).

The field between the plates is uniform, so the electric flux between them is \(\Phi_{E} = EA\). The displacement current is \(\epsilon_{0}\) times the rate of change of this flux:

\(I_{d} = \epsilon_{0}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{E}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \epsilon_{0}A\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

the area of the plates being constant. Substituting,

\(I_{d} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} \times 2 \times 10^{11}\)

\(= 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 4 \times 10^{8}\)

\(\therefore I_{d} = 3.54 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A} = 3.54\text{ mA}\)

Check by following the charge instead of the flux: in \(1\,\mu\text{s}\) the field grows by \(2 \times 10^{11} \times 10^{-6} = 2 \times 10^{5}\text{ V m}^{-1}\), so the surface charge density grows by \(\epsilon_{0} \times 2 \times 10^{5} = 1.77 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C m}^{-2}\) and the charge on a plate by \(1.77 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 3.54 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}\). Delivered in \(10^{-6}\text{ s}\), this is a conduction current of \(3.54 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}\) in the leads, the same value.

**(D)** \(90^{\circ}\)

An electric dipole of moment \(\vec{p}\) placed in a uniform external electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a torque

\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}\), whose magnitude is \(\tau = pE\sin\theta\)

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the dipole moment and the direction of the field.

For a given dipole in a given field \(p\) and \(E\) are fixed, so \(\tau\) is greatest when \(\sin\theta\) is greatest. The greatest value of \(\sin\theta\) is 1, and it occurs at \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), giving

\(\tau_{\max} = pE\)

\(\therefore\) the torque is maximum when the axis of the dipole is perpendicular to the field.

At \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) the torque is zero, that being the position of stable equilibrium; and at the two intermediate angles named, \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5\) and \(\sin 45^{\circ} = 0.707\), both smaller than 1.
twin: An electric dipole consists of two opposite charges each of magnitude \( 1\,\mu\text{C} \) separated by 2 cm. The dipole is placed in an external electric field of \( 10^{5} \) N C\( ^{-1} \). Find: (i) The maximum torque exerted by the field on the dipole (ii) The work the external agent will have to do in turning the dipole through \( 180^\circ \) starting from the position \( \theta = 0^\circ \)

answer:
Given: magnitude of each charge \(q = 1\,\mu\text{C} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}\), separation \(2l = 2\text{ cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}\), external field \(E = 10^{5}\text{ N/C}\).

**Dipole moment.**

\(p = q \times 2l = 1 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-2} = 2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C m}\)

**i. Maximum torque.** The torque on a dipole in a uniform field is \(\tau = pE\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the dipole moment and the field. It is greatest when \(\sin\theta = 1\), that is at \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\):

\(\tau_{\max} = pE\sin 90^{\circ} = 2 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{5} \times 1\)

\(\therefore \tau_{\max} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N m}\)

**ii. Work done in turning the dipole through \(180^{\circ}\).** The dipole is taken to be turned from \(\theta_{1} = 0^{\circ}\), the position of stable equilibrium, to \(\theta_{2} = 180^{\circ}\). The work done in turning a dipole from \(\theta_{1}\) to \(\theta_{2}\) is

\(W = pE\left(\cos\theta_{1} - \cos\theta_{2}\right)\)

\(= 2 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{5}\left(\cos 0^{\circ} - \cos 180^{\circ}\right)\)

\(= 2 \times 10^{-3}\left(1 - (-1)\right)\)

\(\therefore W = 4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\)

This work is done against the field, the dipole ending in the position of unstable equilibrium with its potential energy raised by \(4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\); the field itself therefore does \(-4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\) of work during the rotation.

Check: the potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field is \(U = -pE\cos\theta\), so \(U_{1} = -2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\) at \(\theta_{1} = 0^{\circ}\) and \(U_{2} = +2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\) at \(\theta_{2} = 180^{\circ}\). The rise in potential energy, \(U_{2} - U_{1} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}\), equals the work found above, as it must.
